claims.claim: Within chimpanzee organoids grown for 52 days, cortex-like regions with PAX6-positive APs residing predominantly in the apical-most zone facing a ventricular lumen were observed.
claims.source: Similar to human iPSC-derived cerebral organoids ([Camp et al., 2015], Figure 1B,C right), within the chimpanzee organoids grown for 52 days (D52), we observed cortex-like regions (Figure 1A right) with PAX6-positive APs (such as radial glia) residing predominantly in the apical-most zone facing a ventricular lumen (Figure 1B left), similar to the ventricular zone (VZ) of developing primate neocortex at an early-mid stage of neurogenesis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunohistofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Cells immunoreactive for the deep-layer neuron marker CTIP2 were observed in the basal region of the developing cortical wall in chimpanzee organoids.
claims.source: Consistent with this, cells immunoreactive for the deep-layer neuron marker CTIP2 were observed in the basal region of the developing cortical wall (Figure 1B left), corresponding to an early cortical plate.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunohistofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: TBR2 positive BPs were concentrated in a zone between the PAX6+ progenitors and the CTIP2+ neurons in chimpanzee organoids.
claims.source: TBR2 (also known as EOMES) positive BPs (presumably mostly basal intermediate progenitors) were concentrated in a zone between the PAX6+ progenitors and the CTIP2+ neurons, corresponding to the subventricular zone (SVZ).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunohistofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Apically directed nuclear migration prior to, and basally directed nuclear migration after, mitosis was observed in chimpanzee organoids, consistent with interkinetic nuclear migration.
claims.source: In the context of the time-lapse live imaging of apical mitoses described below, we observed apically directed nuclear migration prior to, and basally directed nuclear migration after, mitosis, consistent with the existence of interkinetic nuclear migration.
claims.evidence: This is based on live imaging observations described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Chimpanzee cerebral organoids recapitulate important aspects of fetal chimpanzee brain development.
claims.source: Our results suggest that chimpanzee cerebral organoids recapitulate important aspects of fetal chimpanzee brain development and allow comparisons with cerebral cortex development in human cerebral organoids and fetal neocortex.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the Results section.

claims.claim: In both human and chimpanzee organoids, there was a decrease in PAX6+TBR2– apically located NSPCs from D28 to D52.
claims.source: In both species, we observed a decrease in PAX6+TBR2– apically located NSPCs (presumably proliferating APs) from D28 to D52, concomitant with an increase in PAX6+TBR2+ and PAX6–TBR2+ basally located NSPCs (presumably neurogenic BPs) (Figure 2A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunohistofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: At D52-D54, the proportion of PAX6+TBR2+ NSPCs in chimpanzee organoids was nearly twice that in human organoids.
claims.source: Notably, whereas no significant differences were observed at D28, at D52-D54, the proportion of PAX6+TBR2+ NSPCs in the chimpanzee organoids was nearly twice that in the human organoids, and the proportion of PAX6+TBR2– NSPCs was correspondingly lower, whereas no significant difference between human and chimpanzee was observed for PAX6–TBR2+ NSPCs (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The proportion of PAX6–TBR2– cells increased from D28 to D52-D54 to about a third of the total cells for both human and chimpanzee cerebral organoids.
claims.source: In line with what would be expected with regard to neuron production, the proportion of PAX6–TBR2– cells, located in the basal-most zones of the developing cortical wall, was very low at D28 but increased by D52-D54 to about a third of the total cells for both, human and chimpanzee cerebral organoids (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The total proportion of NSPCs relative to neurons was virtually identical in human and chimpanzee organoids.
claims.source: Consistent with the observation that the total proportion of NSPCs relative to neurons was virtually identical in human and chimpanzee organoids (Figure 2B), the abundance of cycling cells, as revealed by KI67 immunostaining, was essentially similar (Figure 2C,D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The abundance of cycling cells, as revealed by KI67 immunostaining, was essentially similar in human and chimpanzee organoids.
claims.source: Consistent with the observation that the total proportion of NSPCs relative to neurons was virtually identical in human and chimpanzee organoids (Figure 2B), the abundance of cycling cells, as revealed by KI67 immunostaining, was essentially similar (Figure 2C,D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunohistofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claims.claim: 344 single cell transcriptomes were analysed from 7 chimpanzee organoids ranging in age from 45 to 80 days.
claims.source: To survey the cellular composition and cell type-specific transcriptomes of the chimpanzee organoids, we analysed 344 single cell transcriptomes from 7 organoids ranging in age from 45 to 80 days (Figure 1D, Figure 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design and data collection.

claims.claim: tSNE analysis identified cells into transcriptionally distinct groups representing cerebral cortex, hindbrain, ventral midbrain and peripheral mesenchyme in chimpanzee organoids.
claims.source: Using these genes, we used tSNE analysis to cluster cells into transcriptionally distinct groups representing cerebral cortex, hindbrain, ventral midbrain and peripheral mesenchyme (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by tSNE analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: 178 cortex-like cells were identified in chimpanzee organoids based on expression of canonical NSPC and neuron marker genes.
claims.source: We identified 178 cortex-like cells based on strong expression of canonical NSPC and neuron marker genes (i.e., NSPCs and neurons: FOXG1, NFIA, NFIB; NSPCs: PAX6, SOX2, GLI3; neurons: NEUROD6) and the lack of expression of the ventral and medial telencephalic markers OTX2 and RSPO2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Groups of chimpanzee cells correlated best with one of the four zones (VZ, iSVZ, oSVZ, cortical plate) of human fetal neocortex.
claims.source: We found that groups of cells correlated best with one of the four zones, suggesting that the range of cell types present in the human fetal and organoid cerebral cortex are represented in our chimpanzee data (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Classification of chimpanzee cerebral cortex cells resulted in 73 APs, 25 BPs, and 80 neurons.
claims.source: We next classified the chimpanzee cerebral cortex cells by determining the fetal cell type with which each cell most strongly correlates, resulting in 73 APs, 25 BPs, and 80 neurons.
claims.evidence: This describes the results of cell type classification analysis.

claims.claim: Lineage relationship analysis revealed a structured topology where VZ-APs connect to cortical plate neurons through SVZ-BPs in chimpanzee organoids.
claims.source: We inferred lineage relationships among the chimpanzee cerebral cortex in an adjacency network based on pairwise correlations between cells (Figure 1H), revealing a structured topology where VZ-APs connect to cortical plate neurons through SVZ-BPs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by network analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: In a PCA of human and chimpanzee cells, the first principal component (PC1) separated NSPCs and neurons, whereas PC2 separated species.
claims.source: In a PCA, the first principal component (PC1) separated NSPCs and neurons, whereas PC2 separated species (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Human and chimpanzee organoid and human fetal cells were distributed together within the two main sub-clusters representing NSPCs and neurons.
claims.source: Hierarchical clustering of organoid and fetal cells showed that human and chimpanzee organoid and human fetal cells were distributed together within the two main sub-clusters representing NSPCs and neurons (not shown), and showed highly correlated expression of marker gene patterns (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis and marker gene expression shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: A combined species network revealed that APs, BPs, and neurons from human and chimpanzee intermixed.
claims.source: Generally, APs, BPs, and neurons from human and chimpanzee intermixed, confirming that cells in the chimpanzee organoid cortices have a zonal organization consistent with what is observed histologically (Figure 3C,D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by network analysis shown in Figure 3C,D.

claims.claim: The major proportion of variation in the data is not between in vitro and in vivo tissues or between species, but among cell states during neurogenesis.
claims.source: In conclusion, the major proportion of the variation in these data is not between in vitro and in vivo tissues or between species, but among cell states during neurogenesis, confirming that the major features of the genetic programs regulating the NSPC-to-neuron lineage are conserved between human and chimpanzees, and are recapitulated in cerebral organoids.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative transcriptomics analysis.

claims.claim: 297 genes were more highly expressed in human APs compared to chimpanzee APs.
claims.source: We identified 297 and 279 genes that were more highly expressed in human APs and neurons, respectively, and 283 and 314 genes that were more highly expressed in chimpanzee APs and neurons, respectively (Figure 3E, Figure 3—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: 279 genes were more highly expressed in human neurons compared to chimpanzee neurons.
claims.source: We identified 297 and 279 genes that were more highly expressed in human APs and neurons, respectively, and 283 and 314 genes that were more highly expressed in chimpanzee APs and neurons, respectively (Figure 3E, Figure 3—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: 94% of genes that are AP-specific and neuron-specific in humans are not differential between human and chimpanzee.
claims.source: The vast majority (94%) of genes that are AP-specific and neuron-specific in humans are not differential between human and chimpanzee (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: 93 genes are strongly upregulated in human organoid APs compared to chimpanzee.
claims.source: Of the differentially expressed genes between species, we identified 93 genes that are strongly upregulated in human organoid APs and 72 genes upregulated in human organoid neurons.
claims.evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis.

claims.claim: 72 genes are upregulated in human organoid neurons compared to chimpanzee.
claims.source: Of the differentially expressed genes between species, we identified 93 genes that are strongly upregulated in human organoid APs and 72 genes upregulated in human organoid neurons.
claims.evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis.

claims.claim: ITGB8 is upregulated specific to human APs.
claims.source: Gene ontology enrichments suggest that the proteins encoded by some of these genes are integral to cell membranes and involved in intercellular signalling (Figure 3F, Figure 3—source data 2), for example integrin beta 8 (ITGB8) in APs and insulin receptor (INSR) in human neurons. This upregulation of ITGB8 specific to human APs and INSR specific to human neurons is also observed in comparisons between human and mouse (Florio et al., 2015) (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis and comparison with mouse data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: INSR is upregulated specific to human neurons.
claims.source: Gene ontology enrichments suggest that the proteins encoded by some of these genes are integral to cell membranes and involved in intercellular signalling (Figure 3F, Figure 3—source data 2), for example integrin beta 8 (ITGB8) in APs and insulin receptor (INSR) in human neurons. This upregulation of ITGB8 specific to human APs and INSR specific to human neurons is also observed in comparisons between human and mouse (Florio et al., 2015) (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis and comparison with mouse data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: 75% of the genes with expression specific to APs or neurons in humans are also specific to each cell type in the mouse.
claims.source: When comparing these results to bulk RNA-seq data from mouse APs and neurons (Florio et al., 2015), we find that 75% of the genes with expression specific to APs or neurons in humans are also specific to each cell type in the mouse, suggesting that these gene expression programs were already established and likely present in the common ancestor of mouse, human and chimpanzee some 90 million years ago (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with mouse bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: About 12% of genes specific to APs or neurons in both human and chimpanzee were not specific to these cell types in the mouse.
claims.source: About 12% of these genes specific to AP or neurons in both human and chimpanzee were not specific to these cell types in the mouse (Florio et al., 2015), suggesting that they may be involved in developmental processes specific to the primate cerebral cortex.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with mouse data and suggests evolutionary implications.

claims.claim: Chromosome dynamics and spindle orientation of APs were similar in human developing neocortex and human organoids.
claims.source: Chromosome dynamics and spindle orientation of APs, as revealed by the orientation of the metaphase plate, were similar in human developing neocortex and human organoids, both before anaphase (Figure 4A–D,G) and during anaphase (Figure 4A–D,H,I), when cell cleavage initiates.
claims.evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Cerebral organoids are a suitable model to study live NSPC division and spindle orientation dynamics.
claims.source: This strongly suggests that cerebral organoids are a suitable model to study live NSPC division and spindle orientation dynamics.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of human fetal neocortex and organoid data.

claims.claim: There were no clear differences in spindle orientation between human and chimpanzee APs in cerebral organoids during metaphase.
claims.source: However, our data revealed no clear differences in spindle orientation, either during metaphase (Figure 4C–G) or shortly after anaphase onset (Figure 4C–F, I–J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Most APs in both human and chimpanzee divided with a cleavage orientation largely perpendicular to the apical, ventricular surface.
claims.source: As deduced from the orientation of the chromosome plates, most APs in both human and chimpanzee divided with a cleavage orientation largely perpendicular to the apical, ventricular surface, showing deviations of fewer than 30° from a perfect orthogonal cleavage.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of live imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The frequency of asymmetric cell division caused by oblique spindle orientation is most likely not a major difference between human and chimpanzee APs.
claims.source: This shows that the frequency of asymmetric cell division caused by oblique spindle orientation is most likely not a major difference between human and chimpanzee APs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spindle orientation data.

claims.claim: APs in 11–13 wpc fetal human neocortex and D30 cerebral organoids remained approximately 5 min longer in prometaphase-metaphase than APs in chimpanzee organoids.
claims.source: Specifically, measurement of the length of the various phases of mitosis (for details, see Materials and methods) revealed that APs in 11–13 wpc fetal human neocortex and D30 cerebral organoids remained approximately 5 min longer in prometaphase-metaphase than APs in chimpanzee organoids (Figure 5A–C,E; Video 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by live imaging data and quantification shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Prometaphase-metaphase of APs in mouse neocortex lasted for only approximately half the amount of time than human APs.
claims.source: By comparison, prometaphase-metaphase of APs in slice culture of mouse neocortex, a well-characterized model system for neurogenesis, lasted for only approximately half the amount of time than human APs (Figure 5D,E; Figure 5—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claims.claim: The longer prometaphase-metaphase of human than chimpanzee APs was specifically due to a ~40-60% lengthening of metaphase.
claims.source: Remarkably, the longer prometaphase-metaphase of human than chimpanzee APs was specifically due to a ∼40-60% lengthening of metaphase (Figure 5A–C,G), whereas prometaphase was not significantly different (Figure 5A–C,F; Video 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by live imaging data and quantification shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: In mouse APs, both prometaphase and metaphase were significantly shorter than the respective mitotic phases in human and chimpanzee APs.
claims.source: By contrast, in mouse APs, both prometaphase and metaphase were found to be significantly shorter than the respective mitotic phases in human and chimpanzee APs (Figure 5D,F,G; Figure 5—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: None of the other mitotic phases (prophase, anaphase, telophase) differed in length between APs in human fetal neocortex and human cerebral organoids vs. chimpanzee organoids.
claims.source: None of the other mitotic phases (prophase, anaphase, telophase) differed in length between APs in human fetal neocortex and human cerebral organoids vs. chimpanzee organoids.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Anaphase of mouse APs was significantly shorter than that of human and chimpanzee APs.
claims.source: However, anaphase of mouse APs was found to be significantly shorter than that of human and chimpanzee APs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; Figure 5—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Total mitosis was significantly shorter in mouse APs than human and chimpanzee APs.
claims.source: These differences between species in the individual mitotic phases were reflected in the cumulative length of total mitosis, which was significantly shorter in mouse APs than human and chimpanzee APs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Prometaphase-metaphase and metaphase alone were shorter in D52 than in D30 human APs.
claims.source: Prometaphase-metaphase (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A) and metaphase alone (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C; Figure 5—source data 1) were shorter in D52 than in D30 human APs, and not anymore statistically significantly different in length from D52 chimpanzee APs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The length of prometaphase-metaphase in orangutan D30 organoid APs was similar to that of chimpanzee APs and significantly shorter than that of human organoid APs.
claims.source: This revealed that the length of prometaphase-metaphase in orangutan D30 organoid APs was similar to that of chimpanzee APs and significantly shorter than that of human organoid APs (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The shorter prometaphase-metaphase of orangutan than human APs was due to a shorter metaphase rather than prometaphase.
claims.source: As was the case for the human-chimpanzee AP comparison, the shorter prometaphase-metaphase of orangutan than human APs was due to a shorter metaphase (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,D) rather than prometaphase (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,C; Figure 5—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Human APs specifically lengthen prometaphase-metaphase as compared to great ape APs.
claims.source: Together, these data indicate that human APs specifically lengthen prometaphase-metaphase as compared to great ape APs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of human, chimpanzee, and orangutan data.

claims.claim: Human APs (PAX6+TBR2– cells) exhibited a ~2.7 hr longer cell cycle (46.5 h) than chimpanzee APs (43.8 h).
claims.source: Using cumulative EdU labelling of D52-D54 cerebral organoids (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A), we found a relatively minor (~6%) difference in total cell cycle length, with human APs (PAX6+TBR2– cells) exhibiting a ~2.7 hr longer cell cycle (46.5 h) than chimpanzee APs (43.8 h) (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cumulative EdU labeling data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: S-phase was nearly 5 hr longer in human (17.5 h) than chimpanzee (12.8 h) organoid APs.
claims.source: However, a notable difference between the two species was the length of S-phase, which was nearly 5 hr longer in human (17.5 h) than chimpanzee (12.8 h) organoid APs (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cumulative EdU labeling data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4B.

claims.claim: Both human and chimpanzee organoid APs had a longer prometaphase-metaphase than their respective iPSCs of origin.
claims.source: This revealed that both the human and chimpanzee organoid APs had a longer prometaphase-metaphase than their respective iPSCs of origin, showing that this general lengthening was due to the transition between iPSCs and the organoids of both species (Figure 6A,B,E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: In human APs, the prometaphase-metaphase lengthening was greater than in chimpanzee APs.
claims.source: In human APs, however, the lengthening was greater than in chimpanzee APs.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Human and chimpanzee iPSCs had similar prometaphase-metaphase lengths.
claims.source: In contrast to APs, human and chimpanzee iPSCs had similar prometaphase-metaphase lengths (Figure 6A,B,E; Figure 5—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Both human and chimpanzee APs had a longer prometaphase than their iPSCs of origin.
claims.source: Further dissection into individual phases revealed that, whereas both human and chimpanzee APs had a longer prometaphase than their iPSCs of origin (Figure 6A,B,F), only human APs had a longer metaphase when compared to the iPSCs of origin (Figure 6A,B,G; Figure 5—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Only human APs had a longer metaphase when compared to the iPSCs of origin.
claims.source: Further dissection into individual phases revealed that, whereas both human and chimpanzee APs had a longer prometaphase than their iPSCs of origin (Figure 6A,B,F), only human APs had a longer metaphase when compared to the iPSCs of origin (Figure 6A,B,G; Figure 5—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The length of prometaphase-metaphase in B cells was similar to that in iPSCs.
claims.source: The length of prometaphase-metaphase in B cells, as well as prometaphase and metaphase measured individually, were similar to that in iPSCs (Figure 6 C–G), and hence significantly shorter than in human or chimpanzee APs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Prometaphase-metaphase was longer in proliferative AP divisions (Tis21–) than in neurogenic AP divisions (Tis21+) in mouse.
claims.source: This revealed that prometaphase-metaphase was longer in proliferative AP divisions (Tis21–) than in neurogenic AP divisions (Tis21+ ), whereas the separate phases were not significantly different (Figure 7; Figure 5—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by live imaging data from Tis21::GFP transgenic mice shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: A lengthening of prometaphase-metaphase may be characteristic of proliferating NSPCs.
claims.source: These results suggest that a lengthening of prometaphase-metaphase may be characteristic of proliferating NSPCs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Tis21::GFP mouse data.

claims.claim: Nearly all genes upregulated in human APs in G2-M compared with human APs in G1 were also upregulated during G2-M in iPSCs and endothelial cells.
claims.source: We found that nearly all genes upregulated in human APs in G2-M compared with human APs in G1 were also upregulated during G2-M in iPSCs and endothelial cells (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparative gene expression analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: The expression level of genes upregulated in G2-M is unlikely to contribute to the specificity of mitotic control of human APs in G2-M.
claims.source: Therefore, the expression level of these genes is unlikely to contribute to the specificity of mitotic control of human APs in G2-M.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gene expression analysis.

claims.claim: Genes with the highest specificity score to APs encoded canonical cerebral cortex patterning transcription factors such as PAX6, ID4, and GLI3.
claims.source: Genes with the highest specificity score encoded canonical cerebral cortex patterning transcription factors such as PAX6, ID4, and GLI3, as well as proteins involved in cell adhesion and ECM signalling (CDH4, EFNB1/2, COL4A2).
claims.evidence: This is based on gene expression specificity analysis.

claims.claim: No genes associated with cell cycle, kinetochore, or spindle terms were specific to human APs.
claims.source: Notably, no genes associated with cell cycle, kinetochore, or spindle terms were specific to human APs (Figure 8C, inset).
claims.evidence: This is based on gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: A subset of genes specific to APs were also differentially expressed between human and chimpanzee cerebral organoids (APOLD1, BICC1, EFNB1, GSTM1, IFI44L, ITGB8, SDK2, SEMA5A, SLC35F1, ZNF516).
claims.source: Of genes specific to APs, a subset were also differentially expressed between human and chimpanzee cerebral organoids (APOLD1, BICC1, EFNB1, GSTM1, IFI44L, ITGB8, SDK2, SEMA5A, SLC35F1, ZNF516), which makes them candidates for the unique regulation of AP proliferation in humans (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: The longer prometaphase-metaphase in human than chimpanzee APs may reflect some difference between the two species with regard to the preparation for chromosome segregation.
claims.source: The longer duration of prometaphase-metaphase in human than chimpanzee APs, in particular of the metaphase plate stage (Figure 5B), may therefore reflect some difference between the two species with regard to the preparation for chromosome segregation.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mitotic phase data.

claims.claim: The longer prometaphase-metaphase in human than chimpanzee APs may reflect a greater tendency for proliferative than neurogenic divisions in the human NSPCs.
claims.source: If the longer prometaphase-metaphase in human than chimpanzee APs reflects a greater tendency for proliferative than neurogenic divisions in the human NSPCs, why did we not detect significant differences between human and chimpanzee APs in spindle orientation, a parameter previously shown to affect the mode of AP division (Lancaster and Knoblich, 2012; Mora-Bermudez and Huttner, 2015; Mora-Bermudez et al., 2014; Shitamukai and Matsuzaki, 2012)?
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation discussed in the context of the findings.

claims.claim: Spindle orientation variability between individual APs may be greater than potential inter-species differences.
claims.source: This may be due to spindle orientation variability between individual APs being greater than potential inter-species differences.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of observed differences in spindle orientation.

claims.claim: Differences in proliferative versus neurogenic AP divisions can occur without a change in spindle orientation.
claims.source: Alternatively, this may reflect the fact that differences in proliferative versus neurogenic AP divisions can occur without a change in spindle orientation (Konno et al., 2008; Kosodo et al., 2004; Mora-Bermudez and Huttner, 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Differences between human and chimpanzee NSPCs of relevance for neocortex expansion are likely to be small.
claims.source: In this context, differences between human and chimpanzee NSPCs of relevance for neocortex expansion are likely to be small.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claims.claim: The ~5 min longer prometaphase-metaphase in human than chimpanzee APs constituted only a fraction of the total duration of their mitosis.
claims.source: Furthermore, the ~5 min longer prometaphase-metaphase in human than chimpanzee APs constituted only a fraction of the total duration of their mitosis.
claims.evidence: This is based on the mitotic phase measurements presented in the study.

claims.claim: The accumulation of small differences during evolution may have resulted in the distinct chimpanzee and human neocortices.
claims.source: These small differences nevertheless provide a set of clues as to which NSPC features may underlie the differential extent of neocortex expansion in humans versus apes, and are consistent with a scenario in which the accumulation of such small differences during evolution may have resulted in the distinct chimpanzee and human neocortices.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: Mouse Tis21::GFP-negative APs undergo proliferative divisions to generate more APs.
claims.source: Mouse Tis21::GFP-negative APs, which are known to undergo proliferative divisions to generate more APs, have a longer prometaphase-metaphase than Tis21::GFP-positive APs, which are known to undergo neurogenic divisions to generate BPs (Haubensak et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Mouse Tis21::GFP-positive APs undergo neurogenic divisions to generate BPs.
claims.source: Mouse Tis21::GFP-negative APs, which are known to undergo proliferative divisions to generate more APs, have a longer prometaphase-metaphase than Tis21::GFP-positive APs, which are known to undergo neurogenic divisions to generate BPs (Haubensak et al., 2004).

claims.claim: Mouse Tis21::GFP-negative (proliferative) APs have a longer S-phase than Tis21::GFP-positive (differentiative) APs.

claims.claim: A longer neurogenic period contributes to the greater expansion of the neocortex in humans than the great apes.
claims.source: In sum, two independent lines of evidence, the detailed analysis of AP mitosis phase lengths and the determination of the proportions of the various NSPC types, support the concept that a longer neurogenic period (Lewitus et al., 2014), which in turn implies a longer phase of NSPC proliferation (Otani et al., 2016), contributes to the greater expansion of the neocortex in humans than the great apes.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence and supported by citations.

results.result: Chimpanzee cerebral organoids recapitulate key features of fetal brain development, including cortex-like regions with PAX6+ apical progenitors in the VZ, TBR2+ basal progenitors in the SVZ, CTIP2+ neurons in the cortical plate, and interkinetic nuclear migration.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C23 collectively demonstrate through immunohistofluorescence (Figure 1B,C) and live imaging that chimpanzee organoids exhibit the expected cytoarchitecture and cellular organization of developing primate neocortex. The data show proper spatial organization of cell types and characteristic nuclear migration patterns.

results.result: Single-cell transcriptomics of 344 chimpanzee organoid cells identified 178 cortex-like cells that could be classified into APs, BPs, and neurons, with lineage relationships showing VZ-APs connecting to cortical plate neurons through SVZ-BPs.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C34 describe the single-cell RNA-seq analysis pipeline and results shown in Figure 1. The tSNE clustering, correlation with human fetal zones, cell type classification, and lineage network analysis provide converging evidence for proper cellular composition and developmental trajectories in chimpanzee organoids.

results.result: Human and chimpanzee organoids show remarkably similar cytoarchitecture, cell type composition, and neurogenic gene expression programs, with 94% of cell-type-specific genes conserved between species and the major variation being among cell states during neurogenesis rather than between species.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C35-C38, and C41 are supported by multiple analyses including PCA (Figure 3A), hierarchical clustering (Figure 3B), intercellular correlation networks (Figure 3C,D), and differential expression analysis (Figure 3E). The data consistently show that human and chimpanzee cells intermix by cell type and that the vast majority of developmental programs are conserved.

results.result: A small set of genes are differentially expressed between human and chimpanzee: 297 genes higher in human APs, 279 in human neurons, with 93 strongly upregulated in human APs including ITGB8 and 72 in human neurons including INSR.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C45 are supported by SCDE analysis shown in Figure 3E and validated by comparison with human-mouse data (Figure 3G). The identification of specific differentially expressed genes is based on appropriate statistical methods, though the functional significance of these differences requires further investigation.

results.result: At D52-D54, chimpanzee organoids showed nearly twice the proportion of PAX6+TBR2+ neurogenic basal progenitors compared to human organoids, while the total proportion of NSPCs to neurons and cycling cell abundance were similar between species.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C28 are supported by quantitative immunohistofluorescence data in Figure 2. The statistical analysis shows significant differences in PAX6+TBR2+ cells (p<0.01) while other cell populations remain similar. However, the biological interpretation of this difference requires caution as sample sizes and organoid variability could affect these measurements.

results.result: Spindle orientation dynamics are similar between human fetal neocortex and human organoids, and between human and chimpanzee organoids, with most APs dividing perpendicular to the ventricular surface and no significant differences in oblique divisions between species.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 are supported by live imaging data in Figure 4. The quantification of spindle orientation shows no significant differences between human and chimpanzee APs during metaphase or anaphase. However, the high variability in spindle orientation between individual cells may mask subtle species differences.

results.result: Human APs exhibit approximately 5 minutes longer prometaphase-metaphase than chimpanzee APs, specifically due to a 40-60% lengthening of metaphase, while mouse APs have significantly shorter prometaphase and metaphase than both primate species.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 are strongly supported by live imaging data in Figure 5 with statistical significance (p<0.001). The measurements are based on clear morphological criteria using chromosome dynamics, and the difference is consistently observed across human fetal tissue and organoids. The mouse comparison provides important evolutionary context.

results.result: The prometaphase-metaphase lengthening in human APs is developmentally regulated (shorter at D52 than D30) and human-specific compared to great apes, as orangutan APs show similar timing to chimpanzee APs.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63 are supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3. The developmental regulation and orangutan comparison strengthen the conclusion that metaphase lengthening is a human-specific feature. However, the orangutan data is from only one iPSC line with n=16 cells, which limits the strength of this conclusion.

results.result: Human APs have a 2.7 hour longer total cell cycle (46.5h vs 43.8h) and nearly 5 hours longer S-phase (17.5h vs 12.8h) compared to chimpanzee APs at D52-D54.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 are supported by cumulative EdU labeling data in Figure 5—figure supplement 4. The linear regression analysis provides quantitative estimates of cell cycle parameters. However, the relatively small difference in total cell cycle length (6%) compared to the large difference in S-phase suggests these measurements may be sensitive to experimental conditions.

results.result: The prometaphase-metaphase lengthening occurs during neural differentiation from iPSCs to APs in both species, but is greater in humans. Human and chimpanzee iPSCs and B cells show similar prometaphase-metaphase lengths, suggesting the difference is specific to neural progenitors.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C71 are supported by live imaging data in Figure 6. The comparison across cell types (iPSCs, APs, B cells) demonstrates that the species difference emerges specifically during neural differentiation. This strengthens the conclusion that the metaphase lengthening is functionally related to neural progenitor biology rather than a general cellular difference.

results.result: In mouse, proliferative APs (Tis21::GFP-negative) have longer prometaphase-metaphase than neurogenic APs (Tis21::GFP-positive), suggesting that prometaphase-metaphase lengthening is characteristic of proliferating NSPCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 and C86-C87 are supported by live imaging data from Tis21::GFP transgenic mice in Figure 7. The use of a validated marker of neurogenic vs proliferative divisions provides functional context for the prometaphase-metaphase measurements. However, the difference is modest (p<0.05) and the separate phases are not significantly different.

results.result: Genes upregulated in G2-M phase of human APs are also upregulated in iPSCs and endothelial cells, suggesting general cell cycle regulation. However, AP-specific genes include cortical patterning factors (PAX6, ID4, GLI3) and a subset differentially expressed between human and chimpanzee (APOLD1, BICC1, EFNB1, GSTM1, IFI44L, ITGB8, SDK2, SEMA5A, SLC35F1, ZNF516).
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C78 are supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis in Figure 8. The comparison across cell types (APs, iPSCs, endothelial cells) and cell cycle phases provides insight into AP-specific regulation. However, the identification of candidate genes for human-specific AP proliferation is speculative and requires functional validation.

results.result: Multiple lines of evidence support that human APs have greater proliferative capacity than chimpanzee APs: genes upregulated in human APs suggest increased proliferation, the proportion of neurogenic basal progenitors is lower in humans, human APs have longer S-phase, and longer prometaphase-metaphase is associated with proliferative divisions in mouse.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7 and C89-C90 integrate multiple results to support the conclusion that human APs have greater proliferative capacity. The convergence of transcriptomic data (C6), cell type proportions (C7), S-phase length (C89), and functional association with proliferation (C90) provides strong support. However, direct measurement of proliferative vs neurogenic division outcomes in human vs chimpanzee APs would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: 75% of genes with AP- or neuron-specific expression in humans are also cell-type-specific in mouse, suggesting these programs were established in the common ancestor ~90 million years ago, while 12% are specific to primates.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 are supported by comparison with mouse bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3H. The evolutionary interpretation is reasonable given the data, though the comparison between single-cell and bulk RNA-seq data introduces some uncertainty. The primate-specific genes represent interesting candidates for primate cortical development.

results.result: Other mitotic phases (prophase, anaphase, telophase) do not differ between human and chimpanzee APs, though mouse APs have significantly shorter anaphase and total mitosis than primate APs.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C59 are supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1. These negative results are important for demonstrating the specificity of the prometaphase-metaphase difference. The mouse comparison provides evolutionary context showing that total mitosis duration differs between rodents and primates.

results.result: The longer prometaphase-metaphase in human APs may reflect differences in chromosome segregation preparation or greater tendency for proliferative divisions. The small magnitude of differences (~5 min of ~80 min total mitosis) is consistent with subtle evolutionary changes accumulating to produce distinct human and chimpanzee neocortices.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C85 are largely speculative interpretations (C79-C82, C85) or general conclusions (C83-C84) from the data. While the speculation is reasonable and well-contextualized with citations, these claims represent hypotheses rather than demonstrated results. The discussion of why spindle orientation differences were not detected (C80-C82) is thoughtful but uncertain.

results.result: Human neocortex expansion, which likely contributed to human cognitive abilities, involves increased neuron production during fetal development and reflects greater proliferative capacity of neural progenitors.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C8-C10 represent established knowledge in the field supported by multiple citations. These claims provide important context for the study but are not novel findings. The citations to previous literature (Geschwind and Rakic 2013, Rakic 2009, Striedter 2005, Borrell and Reillo 2012, etc.) support these statements.

results.result: The neocortex develops from VZ and SVZ germinal zones containing APs and BPs respectively. Spindle orientation in mitotic APs plays a pivotal role in determining proliferative vs neurogenic divisions. Human cerebral organoids recapitulate key features of fetal neocortex development including germinal zone organization and gene expression programs.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C17 represent established knowledge about neocortex development and cerebral organoids, supported by citations to previous literature. These provide essential background for the study. Claim C17 specifically cites the authors' previous work (Camp et al. 2015) establishing the validity of organoids as a model system.

results.result: In mouse, proliferative APs (Tis21::GFP-negative) have longer S-phase than differentiative APs (Tis21::GFP-positive).
results.evaluation: Claim C88 is supported by citation to Arai et al. 2011. This prior knowledge is used to interpret the longer S-phase observed in human vs chimpanzee APs (C89) as consistent with greater proliferative capacity in humans.
